chem_edx.6.0.summary: Elements are grouped in the periodic table by their electronic configuration: elements in the same **group** have the **same number of electrons in their outer shell**, so they have **similar chemical properties**. **Group 1** elements (the **alkali metals**) have one outer electron, **group 7** elements (the **halogens**) have seven outer electrons, and **group 0** elements (the **noble gases**) have a **full outer shell**. You must be able to explain why an element belongs to one of these groups from its position in the table or its electronic configuration.

core.h: Groups and periods in the periodic table
core.p: The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing **atomic number** (number of protons). The vertical columns are called **groups** and the horizontal rows are called **periods**. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties, which is why the table is so useful for predicting how an element will behave.
bullets: **Groups** are the vertical columns; **periods** are the horizontal rows.
**Group 1** is the column on the far left: the **alkali metals** (lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, francium).
**Group 7** is the column second from the right: the **halogens** (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine).
**Group 0** is the column on the far right: the **noble gases** (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon).
Metals are found on the left and in the centre; non-metals are on the right, so group 1 are metals while groups 7 and 0 are non-metals.
The **transition metals** sit in the central block between group 2 and group 3.

callouts.p: Far-left column = group 1 alkali metals; second column from the right = group 7 halogens; far-right column = group 0 noble gases.

core.p: The reason elements are placed in groups is their **electronic configuration**. For groups 1 to 7, the **group number equals the number of electrons in the outer shell**. The **period number equals the number of occupied shells**. Group 0 is different: these elements have a **full outer shell** (8 electrons, or 2 for helium).
bullets: Lithium 2.1, sodium 2.8.1, potassium 2.8.8.1: all have **1 outer electron**, so all are in group 1.
Fluorine 2.7, chlorine 2.8.7: both have **7 outer electrons**, so both are in group 7.
Helium 2, neon 2.8, argon 2.8.8: all have a **full outer shell**, so all are in group 0.
Sodium has 3 occupied shells, so it is in **period 3**; potassium has 4, so it is in **period 4**.
The last number in the electronic configuration tells you the group (for groups 1 to 7).

core.h: Why elements in a group have similar properties
core.p: Chemical reactions involve the **outer electrons** of atoms: atoms react by losing, gaining or sharing them. Because every element in a group has the **same number of outer electrons**, they all react in a **similar way**. This is the key idea behind classifying elements into groups.
bullets: Reactions involve the transfer or sharing of **outer shell electrons**.
Same number of outer electrons means **similar chemical reactions** and similar types of compound.
For example, all group 1 metals react with water to form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen.
All group 7 elements react with metals to form salts containing halide ions.
Properties are similar but not identical: there are **trends** down each group (covered in other spec points).

callouts.p: If asked why elements in a group have similar chemical properties, the answer is: they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.

core.p: The **alkali metals** are classified together because they are all in **group 1** and have **one electron in their outer shell**. They are named 'alkali' metals because they react with water to form **alkaline** solutions of their metal hydroxides.
bullets: Each has **1 outer electron**, which is lost easily in reactions.
They lose that electron to form ions with a **1+ charge**, e.g. Na → Na+ + e-.
They are **metals**: they conduct electricity and are shiny when freshly cut.
They are unusually **soft** (can be cut with a knife) and have **low densities** and low melting points for metals.
They are **very reactive**, so they are stored under oil to stop them reacting with air and water.
Typical reaction: metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen, e.g. 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2.

callouts.p: The elements in group 1 of the periodic table; they have one electron in their outer shell and react with water to form alkaline hydroxides.

core.h: Hydrogen is not an alkali metal
core.p: Hydrogen has the electronic configuration **1**, so it has one outer electron, and it is often drawn above group 1. However, it is **not** an alkali metal, which is a favourite exam trap.
bullets: Hydrogen is a **non-metal** and a **gas** at room temperature.
It exists as **diatomic molecules**, H2, not as a metal lattice.
It does not react with water to form an alkali.
Many periodic tables, including the Edexcel data sheet, place hydrogen on its own at the top, separate from group 1.

callouts.p: Do not include hydrogen when listing the alkali metals. The first alkali metal is lithium.

core.p: The **halogens** are classified together because they are all in **group 7** and have **seven electrons in their outer shell**. They need to gain just one electron to get a full outer shell, which makes them reactive non-metals.
bullets: Each has **7 outer electrons**.
They gain one electron to form **halide ions** with a **1- charge**, e.g. Cl + e- → Cl-.
They are **non-metals** and exist as **diatomic molecules**: F2, Cl2, Br2, I2.
They have **coloured** vapours and are poisonous.
They react with metals to form **salts**, such as sodium chloride; the name halogen means 'salt-former'.
They can also share electrons to form covalent compounds, e.g. hydrogen chloride, HCl.

callouts.p: The elements in group 7 of the periodic table; they have seven electrons in their outer shell and exist as diatomic molecules.

core.p: The **noble gases** are classified together because they are all in **group 0** and have a **full outer shell** of electrons (8, except helium which has 2). A full outer shell is a **stable** arrangement, so these atoms have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons.
bullets: They have a **full outer shell**: helium 2, neon 2.8, argon 2.8.8.
This makes them **chemically inert** (very unreactive).
They exist as **single atoms** (they are **monatomic**), not molecules.
They are all **colourless gases** at room temperature.
They are **non-metals**.
Helium has only 2 outer electrons but is still in group 0, because its only shell (the first) is **full**.

callouts.p: The elements in group 0 of the periodic table; they have a full outer shell of electrons, so they are very unreactive and exist as single atoms.
Helium has 2 outer electrons, but it is not in group 2. It is in group 0 because its outer shell is full.

core.h: Ions and the full outer shell
core.p: Atoms of groups 1 and 7 react to achieve the **same stable electronic configuration as a noble gas**. This explains why alkali metals form 1+ ions, halogens form 1- ions, and noble gases hardly react at all.
bullets: Sodium 2.8.1 **loses** 1 electron to become Na+ 2.8, the same configuration as neon.
Chlorine 2.8.7 **gains** 1 electron to become Cl- 2.8.8, the same configuration as argon.
Argon 2.8.8 already has a full outer shell, so it does not need to lose or gain electrons.
Losing electrons is **oxidation**; gaining electrons is **reduction**.
When sodium reacts with chlorine, an electron transfers from sodium to chlorine, forming the ionic compound sodium chloride.

callouts.p: Group 1 forms 1+ ions; group 7 forms 1- ions; group 0 does not normally form ions.

core.p: Learn the three groups side by side. Many questions give you one property and ask you to name or explain the group.
bullets: Group 1 and group 7 are both **reactive**, but for opposite reasons: group 1 loses an electron, group 7 gains one.
Group 0 is **unreactive** because the outer shell is already full.
Group 1 elements are **metals**; group 7 and group 0 elements are **non-metals**.
Group 7 elements are **diatomic**; group 0 elements are **monatomic**.

core.p: Exam questions often describe an unfamiliar element, or give its atomic number, and ask you to say which group it belongs to and why. Work it out from the **electronic configuration**.
bullets: Step 1: use the atomic number to find the number of electrons (equal to the number of protons in an atom).
Step 2: write the configuration, filling shells 2, 8, 8 in turn.
Step 3: count the outer electrons: 1 means group 1, 7 means group 7, a full shell means group 0.
Step 4: back this up with properties: soft metal that reacts with water = group 1; coloured diatomic non-metal = group 7; colourless unreactive monatomic gas = group 0.
Always **justify** your answer by referring to the number of outer electrons.

callouts.p: For 'Element X has atomic number 19', write 2.8.8.1, then say: X is in group 1 because it has one electron in its outer shell.

core.p: The **period** tells you how many shells of electrons are occupied. Combined with the group, this pins down exactly where an element sits.
bullets: Period 1 elements (H, He) have 1 shell; period 2 elements have 2 shells; period 3 have 3 shells.
Potassium 2.8.8.1 has 4 shells, so it is in period 4, group 1.
Bromine is in period 4, group 7, so its atoms have 4 shells and 7 outer electrons.
Moving **down** a group adds an extra shell each time, so atoms get **larger**, which causes the reactivity trends in groups 1 and 7.

core.p: Grouping by similar properties was the original idea behind the periodic table. Because group membership depends on outer electrons, knowing an element's group lets chemists **predict** its properties.
bullets: Mendeleev grouped elements with similar properties and left gaps for undiscovered elements.
The noble gases had not been discovered when he made his first table; they were later added as a whole new group, which fitted the pattern.
Later, knowledge of electronic configurations explained why the groups work: same outer electrons, similar properties.
You can predict that an unfamiliar group 1 element such as rubidium will react with water to make an alkaline hydroxide.

callouts.p: Similar properties within a group are caused by the same number of outer electrons.

analogy.p: Think of each group as a team wearing the same shirt. Everyone in the group 1 team carries one 'spare' outer electron they are keen to pass on; everyone in the group 7 team is one short and desperate to grab one; the group 0 team already has a complete kit and is not interested in swapping anything. Because team members have the same 'kit' (outer electrons), they play the game (react) in a similar way. The analogy breaks down because players in a team are not more or less eager depending on their height, whereas atoms further down a group have more shells and so their reactivity changes steadily, and electrons are not owned or swapped by choice.

terms.d: A table of all elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number, with elements of similar properties in the same group.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; also the number of electrons in a neutral atom.
A vertical column of the periodic table; elements in a group have the same number of outer shell electrons.
A horizontal row of the periodic table; the period number equals the number of occupied electron shells.
The arrangement of electrons in shells around the nucleus, e.g. 2.8.1 for sodium.
The highest-energy occupied shell; its electrons take part in chemical reactions.
Group 1 elements; reactive metals with one outer electron that form alkaline hydroxides with water.
Group 7 elements; reactive non-metals with seven outer electrons that exist as diatomic molecules.
Group 0 elements; unreactive, monatomic gases with a full outer shell.
An outer shell holding the maximum number of electrons (2 for the first shell, 8 for the next shells at GCSE), giving a stable arrangement.
Chemically unreactive.
Made of molecules containing two atoms, e.g. Cl2.
Existing as single, separate atoms, e.g. Ne.
An atom or group of atoms with an electrical charge, formed by losing or gaining electrons.
A negative ion with a 1- charge formed from a halogen atom, e.g. Cl-, Br-.
The block of metals in the centre of the periodic table, between groups 2 and 3.

mistakes.w: Elements in the same group have the same number of shells
mistakes.r: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons; the number of shells is the period.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen is an alkali metal because it has one outer electron
mistakes.r: Hydrogen is a non-metal gas, not an alkali metal; group 1 alkali metals start at lithium.

mistakes.w: Helium is in group 2 because it has 2 outer electrons
mistakes.r: Helium is in group 0 because its outer shell is full.

mistakes.w: Noble gases are unreactive because they have 8 electrons
mistakes.r: Noble gases are unreactive because they have a full outer shell (helium has only 2), so they do not need to lose, gain or share electrons.

mistakes.w: Halogens lose seven electrons to get a full shell
mistakes.r: Halogens gain one electron to form 1- ions with a full outer shell.

mistakes.w: Group 1 elements form 1- ions
mistakes.r: Group 1 atoms lose one electron, forming 1+ ions such as Na+.

mistakes.w: Chlorine exists as single Cl atoms
mistakes.r: Halogens are diatomic molecules: Cl2. Noble gases are the ones that exist as single atoms.

mistakes.w: Elements in a group have the same properties
mistakes.r: They have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of outer electrons, but there are trends down the group.

mistakes.w: Alkali metals are so called because they are alkaline
mistakes.r: They react with water to form metal hydroxides, which dissolve to give alkaline solutions.

exam.q: Name the group in the periodic table that contains the halogens.
model: Group 7.
exam.tip: Halogens = group 7; noble gases = group 0.

exam.q: Give the name used for the elements in group 1.
model: Alkali metals.
exam.tip: Not 'alkaline metals' or 'alkaline earth metals' (that is group 2).

exam.q: Potassium has the electronic configuration 2.8.8.1. Explain why potassium is placed in group 1.
model: Potassium has one electron in its outer shell.
Group 1 elements have one outer electron (group number = number of outer electrons).
exam.tip: Point to the final number in the configuration.

exam.q: Explain why lithium, sodium and potassium have similar chemical properties.
model: They are all in the same group / group 1.
They all have the same number of electrons (one) in their outer shell.
exam.tip: The outer electrons are what take part in reactions.

exam.q: Element X has atomic number 9. State which group X is in and explain your answer.
model: Group 7.
Electronic configuration 2.7, so it has 7 electrons in its outer shell.
exam.tip: Write the configuration first, then the group.

exam.q: Explain why argon is classified as a noble gas.
model: Argon has a full outer shell (2.8.8).
So it is very unreactive / does not need to lose, gain or share electrons; it is in group 0.
exam.tip: Full outer shell is the key phrase.

exam.q: Helium has only two electrons. Explain why helium is placed in group 0 and not in group 2.
model: Helium's only (first) shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons, so its outer shell is full.
Group 0 elements have full outer shells and are unreactive, like helium; group 2 metals are reactive.
exam.tip: Mention that the first shell holds only 2.

exam.q: Describe the difference between how sodium atoms and chlorine atoms form ions. Use electronic configurations in your answer.
model: Sodium is 2.8.1 and chlorine is 2.8.7.
Sodium loses one electron to form Na+ (2.8).
Chlorine gains one electron to form Cl- (2.8.8).
Both ions have a full outer shell / the electronic configuration of a noble gas.
exam.tip: Give the ion charges and the new configurations.

exam.q: Element Z is a soft, shiny solid that reacts vigorously with water, forming an alkaline solution and hydrogen. Suggest which group Z is in and how many outer electrons it has.
model: Group 1 (alkali metals).
One outer electron.
exam.tip: Reacts with water to give an alkaline solution = alkali metal.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of electronic configurations and position in the periodic table, why elements are classified as alkali metals, halogens or noble gases.
model: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer shell electrons, so they have similar chemical properties.
Alkali metals are in group 1 (far left) and have one outer electron, e.g. sodium 2.8.1.
Alkali metals lose this electron to form 1+ ions / are reactive metals that form alkaline hydroxides with water.
Halogens are in group 7 (second from right) and have seven outer electrons, e.g. chlorine 2.8.7.
Halogens gain one electron to form 1- ions / are reactive non-metals existing as diatomic molecules.
Noble gases are in group 0 (far right) and have a full outer shell, e.g. argon 2.8.8, so they are unreactive and monatomic.
exam.tip: Cover all three groups: position, outer electrons, an example configuration and a linked property.

worked.q: An element has atomic number 17. Identify its group and period, and explain whether it is an alkali metal, halogen or noble gas.
steps: Atomic number 17 means 17 protons, so a neutral atom has 17 electrons.
Fill the shells: first shell 2, second shell 8, third shell 7, giving 2.8.7.
There are 7 outer electrons, so the element is in group 7.
There are 3 occupied shells, so it is in period 3.
Group 7 elements are the halogens; this element is chlorine.
worked.ans: Group 7, period 3: a halogen (chlorine), because it has seven electrons in its outer shell.

worked.q: Classify each element: A has configuration 2.8.8; B has configuration 2.8.8.1; C has configuration 2.7.
steps: A: 2.8.8 has a full outer shell, so A is in group 0, a noble gas (argon).
B: 2.8.8.1 has one outer electron, so B is in group 1, an alkali metal (potassium, period 4).
C: 2.7 has seven outer electrons, so C is in group 7, a halogen (fluorine, period 2).
In each case the classification is justified by the number of outer electrons.
worked.ans: A = noble gas (group 0), B = alkali metal (group 1), C = halogen (group 7).

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why neon does not react, but sodium and fluorine do.
steps: Neon is 2.8: it has a full outer shell, which is stable, so it does not need to lose, gain or share electrons. It is inert.
Sodium is 2.8.1: it has one outer electron that it loses easily to form Na+ with a full outer shell.
Fluorine is 2.7: it needs to gain one electron to form F- with a full outer shell.
So sodium and fluorine react (for example with each other, transferring an electron), while neon does not.
worked.ans: Neon has a full outer shell so is unreactive; sodium and fluorine do not, so they react by losing or gaining one electron to achieve a full outer shell.

chem_edx.6.1.summary: The Group 1 elements (lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium) are called the **alkali metals**. They are **soft** metals with **relatively low melting points** that react vigorously with water to form an **alkaline metal hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas**. Going **down the group they get more reactive**, because the single outer electron is **further from the nucleus and more shielded**, so it is **lost more easily**. You must be able to describe the reactions of lithium, sodium and potassium with water, use observations to spot the pattern, and explain it from electronic configurations.

core.h: Where Group 1 is and why it is called the alkali metals
core.p: Group 1 is the first column on the left of the periodic table. Every element in it has **one electron in its outer shell**, which is why they all behave in such a similar way. They are called the **alkali metals** because they react with water to make **alkaline** solutions of their hydroxides.
bullets: Members: lithium (Li), sodium (Na), potassium (K), rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs) and francium (Fr).
Electronic configurations: Li **2.1**, Na **2.8.1**, K **2.8.8.1** - always one outer electron.
Group number = number of outer-shell electrons, so Group 1 = 1 outer electron.
Hydrogen sits above Group 1 in some tables but it is **not** an alkali metal (it is a non-metal gas).
They are so reactive that they are **never found uncombined** in nature - only in compounds such as sodium chloride.

callouts.p: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they have **similar chemical properties**. In Group 1 every atom reacts by **losing its one outer electron** to form a **1+ ion**.

core.h: Physical properties: soft with low melting points
core.p: The Edexcel specification asks you to explain why the alkali metals are classified as metals and to describe them as **soft** with **relatively low melting points**. They are unusual metals: most metals are hard and have high melting points, but Group 1 metals can be cut with a knife.
bullets: **Soft** - can be cut with a scalpel or knife; softness **increases** down the group (potassium is softer than lithium).
**Relatively low melting points** compared with most metals (e.g. iron melts at about 1538 °C, sodium at about 98 °C).
Melting points **decrease** down the group: Li about 181 °C, Na about 98 °C, K about 63 °C.
**Low density** - lithium, sodium and potassium all **float on water** (density less than 1 g/cm3).
Typical metal properties too: **shiny when freshly cut**, **good conductors** of heat and electricity.
Freshly cut surfaces **tarnish quickly** in air as the metal reacts with oxygen to form a dull oxide layer.

Melting point (°C, approx.)

rows: Hardest of the three, still cuts

callouts.p: Density generally increases down the group, but **potassium is less dense than sodium**. Do not claim a perfect density pattern; the safe trends to quote are melting point decreasing and reactivity increasing.

core.h: Why they are classed as metals
core.p: Even though they are soft and melt easily, the alkali metals are definitely metals. They show the key metallic properties and, chemically, they form **positive ions** by **losing electrons**, which is the hallmark of a metal.
bullets: They **conduct electricity** and heat (they have delocalised electrons in metallic bonding).
They are **shiny** when freshly cut.
They react by **losing electrons** to form **positive ions** (Li+, Na+, K+).
They form **ionic compounds** with non-metals, e.g. sodium chloride NaCl.
Their oxides and hydroxides are **basic/alkaline**, as metal oxides and hydroxides typically are.

callouts.p: Each atom donates only **one** delocalised electron and the atoms are large, so the **metallic bonding is weak**. Less energy is needed to overcome the attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons, so the melting point is low. Down the group the ions get bigger, the bonding gets weaker and the melting point falls.

core.p: Because they react with both oxygen and water vapour in the air, alkali metals must be stored carefully and handled with care in the lab.
bullets: Stored **under oil** (paraffin oil) to keep out air and moisture.
Handled with **tongs**, never fingers - moisture on skin reacts with the metal.
Only **small pieces** (about the size of a rice grain) are used in water reactions.
Use a **safety screen** and wear **safety goggles**, especially for potassium.
The product hydroxides are **corrosive** and hydrogen is **flammable**.

callouts.t: Do not say they are stored in water
callouts.p: They are stored **under oil**, because they react with water. Stored in water they would fizz away and could catch fire.

core.h: Reaction with water: the general equation
core.p: All the alkali metals react with cold water. The products are always a **metal hydroxide** (which dissolves to give an **alkaline solution**) and **hydrogen gas**.
bullets: Word equation: **metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen**.
Lithium: 2Li(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2LiOH(aq) + H2(g)
Sodium: 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g)
Potassium: 2K(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2KOH(aq) + H2(g)
The same pattern works for any Group 1 metal, e.g. 2Rb + 2H2O → 2RbOH + H2.
Ionic equation (Higher): 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2Na+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) + H2(g).

callouts.p: Hydrogen is diatomic (H2), so you need **2** metal atoms and **2** water molecules to make **1** H2. The ratio is always 2 : 2 : 2 : 1.
A **soluble base** that forms **hydroxide ions, OH-(aq)**, in water. Solutions of alkali metal hydroxides have a **pH greater than 7**.

core.p: Lithium is the least reactive of the three metals you need to know. The reaction is steady and gentle enough to watch easily.
bullets: **Floats** on the water (less dense than water).
**Fizzes steadily** - bubbles of hydrogen gas are given off.
Moves slowly around the surface.
Does **not melt** - stays as a solid piece.
Gradually gets **smaller and disappears** as it reacts.
Universal indicator added to the water turns **purple/blue** - an alkaline solution of lithium hydroxide forms.

core.p: Sodium reacts more vigorously than lithium. Enough heat is released to melt the sodium because its melting point (about 98 °C) is low.
bullets: **Floats** on the surface.
**Fizzes rapidly** - hydrogen is given off quickly.
**Melts into a shiny silvery ball** - the reaction is exothermic and sodium has a low melting point.
**Moves (whizzes) quickly** around the surface, pushed by the hydrogen produced.
Usually does not ignite, though it may occasionally produce a yellow-orange flame.
Disappears quickly; indicator turns **purple** (sodium hydroxide is alkaline).

callouts.p: The reaction is **exothermic** (gives out heat). Sodium's melting point is below 100 °C, so the heat released is enough to melt it. Lithium's higher melting point and slower reaction mean it does not melt.

core.p: Potassium is the most reactive of the three. The reaction is violent and the hydrogen produced catches fire.
bullets: **Floats** and **melts** almost instantly into a ball.
Fizzes **very vigorously**; moves around extremely fast.
The heat produced **ignites the hydrogen** - a **lilac (purple) flame** is seen.
May **spit, crackle or explode** at the end of the reaction.
Disappears within seconds; indicator turns **purple** (potassium hydroxide is alkaline).
Rubidium and caesium (not used in schools) react **explosively** with water.

core.h: Using observations to find the reactivity pattern
core.p: Spec point 6.4 asks you to **predict properties from given trends** and to use observations to describe the pattern. The observations above show the reaction getting **more vigorous** from lithium to sodium to potassium, so **reactivity increases down the group**.
bullets: Evidence for increasing reactivity: **faster fizzing**, **melting**, **faster movement**, **flame**, **shorter time** to disappear.
Prediction for rubidium: reacts **more violently than potassium**, explosively, forming rubidium hydroxide RbOH and hydrogen.
Prediction for caesium: **even more violent** than rubidium; lowest melting point (about 28 °C).
Melting point continues to **decrease** down the group, so rubidium melts below 63 °C.
All predicted products are the same type: alkaline hydroxide solution + hydrogen.
Always quote evidence from the **observations**, not just 'it is more reactive'.

callouts.p: If a question gives you data for Li, Na and K and asks about Rb or Cs, **continue the trend** in the same direction and say what you would **see** (e.g. 'explodes', 'melts instantly', 'ignites').

core.h: Explaining the trend from electronic configuration
core.p: Spec point 6.5 asks you to explain the reactivity trend. When an alkali metal reacts it **loses its single outer electron** to form a 1+ ion. The easier this electron is lost, the more reactive the metal. Going down the group, the outer electron is lost more easily.
bullets: Going down the group, atoms have **more occupied electron shells**, so the atoms are **larger**.
The outer electron is **further from the nucleus**.
There is **more shielding** by the inner shells of electrons.
So the **attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker**.
The outer electron is therefore **lost more easily**, so the metal is **more reactive**.
Half equations (Higher): Li → Li+ + e-, Na → Na+ + e-, K → K+ + e-.

callouts.t: The four-step chain for full marks
callouts.p: **More shells → outer electron further from nucleus (and more shielded) → weaker attraction to the nucleus → electron lost more easily → more reactive.**
Do not say the nucleus gets weaker. The number of protons **increases** down the group, but the extra distance and shielding **outweigh** this, so the outer electron is held less strongly overall.

core.h: Oxidation and the formation of ions
core.p: In every reaction of an alkali metal, the metal atom **loses an electron**. Losing electrons is **oxidation**, so the alkali metals are oxidised when they react with water.
bullets: OIL RIG: **Oxidation Is Loss** of electrons, **Reduction Is Gain**.
Na atom 2.8.1 → Na+ ion **[2.8]+** - now has a full outer shell like neon.
K atom 2.8.8.1 → K+ ion **[2.8.8]+** - same electron arrangement as argon.
The ion formed always has a charge of **+1**.
The compounds formed (LiOH, NaOH, KOH) are **ionic** and dissolve to release OH- ions.

core.p: A top answer connects structure, observations and explanation. Use this checklist when writing a 6-mark answer on Group 1.
bullets: State the **trend**: reactivity increases down the group.
Give **observations** for Li, Na and K as evidence (fizzing rate, melting, flame).
Name the **products**: metal hydroxide (alkaline) and hydrogen; write a balanced equation.
Explain with **electronic configuration**: one outer electron, further from nucleus, more shielding, weaker attraction, lost more easily.
Mention physical properties if asked: soft, low melting point, low density, float on water.
Use the correct words: **'lost'** electron (not 'gained'), **'shielding'**, **'attraction'**.

analogy.t: The loose balloon at a party
analogy.p: Imagine each atom is a child holding a balloon (the outer electron) on a string, with the nucleus as the child's hand. Lithium holds its balloon on a very short string close to its hand, so it is hard to snatch. Potassium holds its balloon on a much longer string with a crowd of other children (inner shells) in the way, so it is easily pulled away. The easier the balloon is taken, the more reactive the metal. Where it breaks down: real electrons are not tied on strings, the attraction is an electrostatic force that weakens with distance, and shielding is caused by repulsion from inner electrons, not people physically blocking the way.

terms.d: The elements in Group 1 of the periodic table (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr).
A vertical column of the periodic table; elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons.
The highest occupied energy level of an atom; Group 1 atoms have one electron in it.
The arrangement of electrons in shells, e.g. sodium 2.8.1.
A soluble base that produces hydroxide ions, OH-, in water, giving a solution with pH above 7.
An ionic compound of a metal ion and hydroxide ions, e.g. sodium hydroxide NaOH, formed when an alkali metal reacts with water.
The flammable gas H2 given off when an alkali metal reacts with water; it burns with a squeaky pop.
How readily an element takes part in chemical reactions; for Group 1, how easily the atom loses its outer electron.
The reduction in attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons caused by inner shells of electrons.
The electrostatic attraction between the positive nucleus and the negative electrons.
A charged particle formed when an atom loses or gains electrons; alkali metals form 1+ ions.
Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen); alkali metals are oxidised when they react.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings; the heat from sodium and water melts the sodium.
Loss of shine when a freshly cut metal surface reacts with oxygen in the air to form an oxide layer.
Mass per unit volume; Li, Na and K are less dense than water so they float.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid; for Group 1 it decreases down the group.

mistakes.w: Reactivity increases down the group because the atoms gain electrons more easily.
mistakes.r: Group 1 atoms **lose** their outer electron; it is lost more easily down the group.

mistakes.w: The outer electron is further away so the nucleus is weaker.
mistakes.r: The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the **attraction** between nucleus and outer electron is weaker.

mistakes.w: Sodium + water → sodium oxide + hydrogen.
mistakes.r: The product is **sodium hydroxide** (NaOH) and hydrogen.

mistakes.w: Potassium burns with an orange flame.
mistakes.r: Potassium (the hydrogen it ignites) gives a **lilac** flame.

mistakes.w: The solution formed is acidic.
mistakes.r: The metal hydroxide solution is **alkaline**, pH above 7; universal indicator turns purple.

mistakes.w: Na + H2O → NaOH + H2
mistakes.r: Must be balanced: **2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2**.

mistakes.w: Alkali metals are stored in water to stop them reacting.
mistakes.r: They are stored **under oil** to keep out air and water.

mistakes.w: Observations: 'hydrogen is produced'.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen is a product, not an observation; the observation is **fizzing / bubbles / effervescence**.

mistakes.w: Melting point increases down the group.
mistakes.r: Melting point **decreases** down Group 1.

exam.q: State the number of electrons in the outer shell of a potassium atom.
model: 1 (one)
exam.tip: Group number tells you the number of outer electrons.

exam.q: Give two physical properties of the alkali metals that are unusual for metals.
model: Soft / can be cut with a knife
Low melting point / low density / float on water
exam.tip: Edexcel stresses 'soft' and 'relatively low melting points'.

exam.q: Write the word equation for the reaction of lithium with water.
model: lithium + water → lithium hydroxide + hydrogen
exam.tip: Hydroxide, not oxide.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of sodium with water.
model: Correct formulae: Na, H2O, NaOH, H2
Balanced: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2
State symbols: (s) + (l) → (aq) + (g)
exam.tip: Remember H2 is diatomic, so double the metal and water.

exam.q: A small piece of sodium is added to water containing universal indicator. Describe two things you would see.
model: Fizzing / bubbles / effervescence
Melts into a ball / floats / moves around / indicator turns purple or blue
exam.tip: Describe what you see, not what is made.

exam.q: Explain why the solution turns universal indicator purple after potassium reacts with water.
model: Potassium hydroxide is formed
It is an alkali / produces OH- ions / pH above 7
exam.tip: Link the colour to the product and its pH.

exam.q: Predict how rubidium would react with water, compared with potassium. Give the products.
model: More vigorous / violent / explosive than potassium
Rubidium hydroxide formed
Hydrogen formed
exam.tip: Continue the trend and name the products using the general equation.

exam.q: Describe how the melting point changes down Group 1 and suggest a value for rubidium given Li 181 °C, Na 98 °C, K 63 °C.
model: Melting point decreases down the group
Any value below 63 °C (actual about 39 °C)
exam.tip: Predictions just need to follow the trend sensibly.

exam.q: Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium. Refer to electronic configurations.
model: Potassium 2.8.8.1 has more shells than sodium 2.8.1
Outer electron further from the nucleus / more shielding
Weaker attraction between nucleus and outer electron
Outer electron lost more easily
exam.tip: Use the chain: shells → distance/shielding → attraction → lost more easily.

exam.q: Lithium, sodium and potassium are each added to water. Describe the observations and explain the trend in reactivity in terms of electronic configuration.
model: All float and fizz / produce bubbles of hydrogen
Lithium fizzes steadily and does not melt
Sodium fizzes rapidly, melts into a ball and moves quickly
Potassium reacts violently, melts and burns with a lilac flame
Reactivity increases down the group; each forms an alkaline hydroxide solution and hydrogen
Outer electron further from nucleus with more shielding, weaker attraction, lost more easily
exam.tip: Level-marked: you need both observations AND explanation for the top band.

exam.q: Write a half equation to show what happens to a sodium atom when it reacts. (Higher)
model: Na → Na+ + e-
exam.tip: Electrons appear on the right because they are lost.

worked.q: Caesium is below rubidium in Group 1. Predict and explain its reaction with water and write a balanced equation.
steps: Caesium is lower in Group 1 than potassium and rubidium, so continue the trend: it is the most reactive of these.
Prediction: it would react explosively, instantly melting and igniting the hydrogen.
Products follow the general equation: metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen, so caesium hydroxide and hydrogen.
Formulae: caesium forms Cs+ so the hydroxide is CsOH; hydrogen is H2.
Balance: 2Cs + 2H2O → 2CsOH + H2.
Explanation: caesium has more shells, so its outer electron is much further from the nucleus and heavily shielded, giving a very weak attraction; it is lost extremely easily.
worked.ans: Caesium reacts explosively: 2Cs + 2H2O → 2CsOH + H2, forming an alkaline solution, because its outer electron is lost very easily.

worked.q: A student times how long 0.05 g pieces of Li, Na and K take to disappear in water: Li 95 s, Na 20 s, K 4 s. What do the results show, and what would you predict for rubidium?
steps: A shorter time means a faster reaction, so a more reactive metal.
Order of time: Li (95 s) > Na (20 s) > K (4 s), so reactivity is K > Na > Li.
Li, Na, K are in order down the group, so reactivity increases down the group.
Rubidium is below potassium, so it should react faster still.
Predict a time shorter than 4 s (it may explode).
worked.ans: Reactivity increases down Group 1; rubidium would take less than 4 s (react even faster, explosively).

worked.q: Model answer: explain why lithium is less reactive than sodium (4 marks).
steps: Lithium 2.1 has two shells; sodium 2.8.1 has three shells.
Lithium's outer electron is closer to the nucleus and less shielded by inner electrons.
So there is a stronger attraction between the nucleus and lithium's outer electron.
So more energy is needed to remove it; it is lost less easily than sodium's.
worked.ans: Lithium's outer electron is closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so it is held more strongly and lost less easily, making lithium less reactive.

chem_edx.6.2.summary: The Group 7 elements are the **halogens**: non-metals that exist as **diatomic molecules** (F2, Cl2, Br2, I2). At room temperature **chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas**, **bromine is a red-brown liquid** and **iodine is a grey-black solid** that gives a purple vapour. Going **down the group** the halogens get **darker in colour** and their **melting and boiling points increase**, so you can predict the properties of fluorine and astatine from the trend. Chlorine is identified by the test in which **damp blue litmus paper is bleached (turns white)**.

core.p: Group 7 is the second column from the right of the periodic table. Its elements are called the **halogens**, which means 'salt formers', because they react with metals to make salts such as sodium chloride. All halogens have **seven electrons in their outer shell**.
bullets: Members: fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), iodine (I), astatine (At).
Electronic configurations: F **2.7**, Cl **2.8.7**.
All are **non-metals**: poor conductors, low melting and boiling points.
They exist as **diatomic molecules** - two atoms joined by a single **covalent bond**: F2, Cl2, Br2, I2.
They are **toxic**, so experiments with them are done in a **fume cupboard**.

callouts.p: A molecule made of **two atoms** joined together, e.g. Cl2. Always write halogen elements as **X2** in equations.

core.h: Colours and physical states at room temperature
core.p: Spec point 6.6 requires you to **recall the colours and physical states of chlorine, bromine and iodine at room temperature**. Room temperature is about 20 °C. These three are the ones that come up again and again.
bullets: **Chlorine, Cl2**: **pale yellow-green gas** (often just 'green gas' - say yellow-green to be safe).
**Bromine, Br2**: **red-brown liquid** that gives off an **orange/brown vapour** easily.
**Iodine, I2**: **grey-black (dark grey) solid** with a shiny look; it **sublimes** on warming to give a **purple vapour**.
Fluorine, F2 (for context): **pale yellow gas**.
Astatine (predicted): **black solid** - it is radioactive and extremely rare.

callouts.t: The three to learn word for word
callouts.p: **Chlorine - green (yellow-green) gas. Bromine - red-brown liquid. Iodine - grey-black solid.**

core.p: Halogens dissolve a little in water. The colours of the solutions are useful later when you study displacement reactions, so it helps to know them now.
bullets: **Chlorine water**: very pale green, almost colourless.
**Bromine water**: **orange** (yellow-orange when dilute).
**Iodine solution**: **brown** (dark brown when concentrated).
Iodine is only slightly soluble in water; it dissolves better in potassium iodide solution.
Halide ions (Cl-, Br-, I-) in solution are **colourless** - only the halogen molecules are coloured.

callouts.p: Iodine is a grey-black **solid** but a **brown solution** and a **purple vapour**. Read the question carefully to see which one is asked for.

core.h: Trend 1: colour gets darker down the group
core.p: Going down Group 7, the colour of the halogens becomes **darker**: pale yellow → yellow-green → red-brown → grey-black → black.
bullets: Fluorine is palest; astatine is darkest.
This lets you **predict** the colour of an unfamiliar halogen: astatine is expected to be **black**.
Colour depth increases with the size of the molecule.
Use 'darker' as the trend word - examiners reward it.
Do not confuse colour with reactivity: the darkest halogens are the **least** reactive.

core.h: Trend 2: melting and boiling points increase down the group
core.p: The **melting points and boiling points increase down the group**. That is why the state changes from **gas** (F2, Cl2) to **liquid** (Br2) to **solid** (I2, At2) at room temperature.
bullets: Approximate boiling points: F2 -188 °C, Cl2 -34 °C, Br2 59 °C, I2 184 °C.
Approximate melting points: F2 -220 °C, Cl2 -101 °C, Br2 -7 °C, I2 114 °C.
A substance is a **gas** at 20 °C if its boiling point is **below** 20 °C.
A substance is a **liquid** if 20 °C is **between** its melting and boiling points (bromine: -7 to 59 °C).
A substance is a **solid** if its melting point is **above** 20 °C (iodine: 114 °C).
Predicted for astatine: melting and boiling points **higher than iodine's**, so it is a solid.

callouts.p: Compare **room temperature (20 °C)** with the melting point and boiling point. Below the melting point → solid; between the two → liquid; above the boiling point → gas.

core.h: Why melting and boiling points increase
core.p: Halogens are **simple molecular** substances. When they melt or boil, the covalent bonds inside each molecule do **not** break; it is the weak **intermolecular forces** between the molecules that are overcome.
bullets: Down the group the molecules get **larger** (more electrons, bigger relative formula mass).
Larger molecules have **stronger intermolecular forces** between them.
So **more energy** is needed to overcome these forces.
So melting and boiling points **increase** down the group.
The covalent bond within the molecule (e.g. Cl-Cl) is **not** broken when chlorine boils.

callouts.p: Never write 'the covalent bonds get stronger' or 'more bonds break'. Boiling a halogen overcomes the **intermolecular forces** (forces **between** molecules).

core.p: Spec point 6.7 asks you to **use the trends to predict the properties of other halogens**. Exam questions give you a table with a gap, or ask about fluorine or astatine.
bullets: Look at the data **above and below** the gap and choose a value **in between**, following the trend.
Astatine: **black solid**, melting point **above 114 °C**, boiling point **above 184 °C**.
Fluorine: **pale yellow gas**, lower boiling point than chlorine.
Astatine would also exist as diatomic molecules At2 and have 7 outer electrons.
Give a **reason**: 'because it is lower in the group, so the trend continues'.

callouts.p: State the prediction, then justify it with the trend: 'Astatine is a solid because melting point increases down Group 7 and iodine is already a solid.'

core.p: Spec point 6.8: **describe the chemical test for chlorine**. Chlorine **bleaches damp litmus paper**. This is a positive test only chlorine gives among the common lab gases.
bullets: **Method**: hold a piece of **damp blue litmus paper** in the gas (at the mouth of the test tube).
**Result**: the litmus paper turns **red** briefly and then is **bleached white**.
The paper must be **damp**: chlorine dissolves in the water on the paper to form acidic substances, including one that bleaches.
Red litmus is simply **bleached white** (no red stage).
Carry out the test in a **fume cupboard** because chlorine is toxic.
Bleaching is what makes the test specific - other acidic gases turn blue litmus red but do **not** bleach it.

callouts.p: Chlorine **bleaches damp litmus paper**, turning it **white**. (Damp blue litmus turns red, then white.)

callouts.t: Do not mix up the gas tests
callouts.p: Hydrogen: lighted splint, squeaky pop. Oxygen: glowing splint relights. Carbon dioxide: limewater turns milky. Chlorine: **damp litmus bleached**.

core.h: Why the litmus must be damp
core.p: Chlorine reacts with water to form a mixture of acids. One of these (hypochlorous acid, HClO) is a **bleach** that removes the dye from litmus.
bullets: Cl2 + H2O → HCl + HClO
The acids turn blue litmus **red** first.
HClO then **bleaches** the dye, so the paper turns **white**.
Dry litmus paper reacts very slowly, so the test may fail.
This bleaching property is why chlorine is used to treat **drinking water** and in **bleach**.

core.p: Halogens are dangerous, which is often asked about in practical-style questions.
bullets: Chlorine and bromine vapour are **toxic** and irritate the lungs and eyes - use a **fume cupboard**.
Bromine liquid causes **severe burns** - wear gloves and goggles.
Iodine stains skin and is **harmful**.
Fluorine is so reactive and toxic it is not used in school labs.
Use **small amounts** and dilute solutions where possible.

core.p: Each halogen atom has 7 outer electrons and needs one more for a full shell. Two atoms **share a pair of electrons** in a **single covalent bond**, so both get a full outer shell of 8.
bullets: Cl + Cl → Cl2 with one shared pair of electrons.
Each chlorine atom in Cl2 also has **three lone pairs**.
The molecules are **small and simple**, so the halogens have low melting points compared with ionic or giant covalent substances.
The halogens are **poor conductors**: there are no free electrons or ions.
All halogens have similar chemical properties because they all have **7 outer electrons**.

core.p: Most marks on this point come from recall of colours and states, reading trends from data, and the chlorine test. Precise wording matters.
bullets: Colour: say 'yellow-green' for chlorine, 'red-brown' for bromine, 'grey-black' for iodine.
Trend words: 'darker', 'melting/boiling points **increase**'.
Explanation: 'larger molecules, **stronger intermolecular forces**, more energy to overcome'.
Test: 'damp (blue) litmus paper' + 'bleached / turns white'.
Predictions: follow the trend and give a reason.

callouts.p: One mark for the **method** (damp litmus paper), one for the **result** (bleached / white). 'Turns red' on its own scores no mark.

analogy.p: Think of halogen molecules as Velcro balls in a box. Fluorine and chlorine are tiny balls with only a few Velcro hooks, so they barely stick to each other and fly around freely (a gas). Bromine balls are bigger with more hooks, so they cling loosely and slide over each other (a liquid). Iodine balls are big and covered in hooks, so they stick together firmly (a solid). Shaking the box harder (heating) is needed to separate bigger balls. Where it breaks down: intermolecular forces are electrostatic attractions, not physical hooks, and the atoms inside each ball (the covalent bond) stay joined however hard you shake.

terms.d: The elements in Group 7 of the periodic table: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine.
Made of molecules containing two atoms, e.g. Cl2, Br2, I2.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
A substance made of small molecules with strong covalent bonds inside and weak forces between molecules.
Weak forces of attraction between molecules; these are overcome when a halogen melts or boils.
The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid.
The temperature at which a liquid changes to a gas.
About 20 °C; used to decide the physical state of a substance.
Whether a substance is a solid, liquid or gas at a given temperature.
To change directly from a solid to a gas without melting; iodine does this on warming, giving purple vapour.
The gas formed from a substance that is a liquid or solid at room temperature, e.g. orange bromine vapour.
An indicator paper: blue litmus turns red in acid; red litmus turns blue in alkali.
To remove colour; chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white.
A gradual, regular change in a property going down a group.
Poisonous; halogen vapours are toxic so are used in a fume cupboard.

mistakes.w: Bromine is a brown gas.
mistakes.r: Bromine is a **red-brown liquid** at room temperature (its vapour is orange-brown).

mistakes.w: Iodine is a purple solid.
mistakes.r: Iodine is a **grey-black solid**; it gives a **purple vapour**.

mistakes.w: Test for chlorine: blue litmus turns red.
mistakes.r: Damp litmus paper is **bleached / turns white**.

mistakes.w: Chlorine puts out a lighted splint / makes a squeaky pop.
mistakes.r: That is the hydrogen test; chlorine **bleaches damp litmus**.

mistakes.w: Boiling points increase because the covalent bonds get stronger.
mistakes.r: Molecules get larger so **intermolecular forces** get stronger and need more energy to overcome.

mistakes.w: Melting point decreases down Group 7.
mistakes.r: Melting and boiling points **increase** down Group 7 (it is Group 1 where they decrease).

mistakes.w: Colour gets lighter down the group.
mistakes.r: Colour gets **darker** down the group.

mistakes.w: Chlorine is written as Cl in equations.
mistakes.r: Chlorine exists as **Cl2** (diatomic molecules).

mistakes.w: Astatine would be a gas because it is a halogen.
mistakes.r: Astatine would be a **solid**, as melting point increases down the group.

exam.q: State the colour and physical state of bromine at room temperature.
model: Red-brown (accept brown / orange-brown)
Liquid
exam.tip: Two separate marks: colour and state.

exam.q: Give the physical state of iodine at room temperature.
model: Solid
exam.tip: Room temperature is about 20 °C.

exam.q: Describe the test for chlorine gas.
model: Damp (blue) litmus paper
Bleached / turns white
exam.tip: 'Damp' and 'bleached' are the key words.

exam.q: Chlorine has a melting point of -101 °C and boiling point of -34 °C. Explain why chlorine is a gas at room temperature.
model: Room temperature (20 °C) is above its boiling point
So it has already boiled / turned into a gas
exam.tip: Always compare with 20 °C.

exam.q: Describe the trend in colour of the halogens down Group 7.
model: Colour gets darker
exam.tip: One word answer: darker.

exam.q: Predict the physical state and colour of astatine at room temperature. Give a reason.
model: Solid
Black (accept very dark)
Melting point increases / colour darkens down the group; astatine is below iodine
exam.tip: Always justify predictions with the trend.

exam.q: The boiling points are: chlorine -34 °C, iodine 184 °C. Estimate the boiling point of bromine.
model: Any value between -34 °C and 184 °C (actual 59 °C)
exam.tip: Bromine lies between chlorine and iodine so its value lies between theirs.

exam.q: Explain why the boiling points of the halogens increase down the group.
model: Molecules get larger / greater relative formula mass
Intermolecular forces get stronger
More energy needed to overcome the forces
exam.tip: Say 'intermolecular forces', never 'bonds break'.

exam.q: Explain why damp blue litmus paper first turns red and then white in chlorine.
model: Chlorine reacts with/dissolves in water to form acid(s), turning litmus red
Chlorine (or a product, HClO) bleaches the dye, turning it white
exam.tip: Link the damp paper to the reaction with water.

exam.q: Compare the physical properties of chlorine, bromine and iodine and explain the trend shown. Use your knowledge of structure.
model: Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas
Bromine is a red-brown liquid
Iodine is a grey-black solid
Colour gets darker and melting/boiling points increase down the group
Halogens are simple molecular / diatomic substances
Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to melt or boil them
exam.tip: Level-marked: give the observations and the structural explanation.

worked.q: Using the data, decide the state of each halogen at 20 °C: fluorine (mp -220, bp -188), bromine (mp -7, bp 59), iodine (mp 114, bp 184).
steps: Fluorine: 20 °C is above its boiling point (-188 °C), so it has boiled: gas.
Bromine: 20 °C is above its melting point (-7 °C) but below its boiling point (59 °C): liquid.
Iodine: 20 °C is below its melting point (114 °C), so it has not melted: solid.
worked.ans: Fluorine gas, bromine liquid, iodine solid.

worked.q: A student holds damp blue litmus paper over a gas jar. The paper turns red and then white. Identify the gas and explain why the paper had to be damp.
steps: Bleaching of damp litmus is the positive test for chlorine.
The paper turned red because acids formed when chlorine dissolved in the water on the paper.
It then turned white because chlorine/hypochlorous acid bleached the dye.
Dry paper has no water for chlorine to react with, so the test would not work well.
worked.ans: The gas is chlorine; the paper must be damp so chlorine can react with water to form the acidic, bleaching substances.

worked.q: Astatine is below iodine. Predict its boiling point given Cl -34 °C, Br 59 °C, I 184 °C.
steps: Find the trend: boiling point increases down the group.
Differences: Cl to Br = +93 °C; Br to I = +125 °C. The gap is getting bigger.
So astatine should be more than about 184 + 125 = 309 °C.
Any sensible value above 184 °C would score; around 300-340 °C fits the pattern.
worked.ans: About 310 °C or more (any value above 184 °C); astatine would be a solid at room temperature.

chem_edx.6.3.summary: Halogens react with **metals** to form **metal halides** (ionic salts such as sodium chloride and iron(III) chloride), and with **hydrogen** to form **hydrogen halides** such as hydrogen chloride, HCl. The reactions get **less vigorous down Group 7** (chlorine > bromine > iodine), so you can use the pattern to **predict** how fluorine or astatine would react. Hydrogen halides are gases that **dissolve in water to form acidic solutions**, for example hydrogen chloride dissolves to give **hydrochloric acid**, because the molecules release **H+ ions** in water.

core.p: The halogens are reactive non-metals with **7 outer electrons**. In their reactions with metals they **gain one electron** per atom to form **halide ions** (X-), and in their reactions with hydrogen they **share** an electron pair to form covalent hydrogen halide molecules. Spec points 6.9 and 6.10 cover these two reaction types for **chlorine, bromine and iodine**, and using the pattern to predict others.
bullets: **Metal + halogen → metal halide** (a salt).
**Hydrogen + halogen → hydrogen halide** (a gas).
**Hydrogen halide + water → acidic solution**.
Reactions become **less vigorous** going down the group: Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
Halogens are always written as diatomic molecules: Cl2, Br2, I2.

callouts.p: A compound of a halogen with another element; also the name of the **ion** X- (chloride Cl-, bromide Br-, iodide I-). The ending changes from **-ine** to **-ide**.

core.p: The name of a metal halide comes from the metal followed by the halide ending. Halogen → halide: chlorine → **chloride**, bromine → **bromide**, iodine → **iodide**, fluorine → **fluoride**.
bullets: Sodium + chlorine → **sodium chloride**, NaCl.
Potassium + bromine → **potassium bromide**, KBr.
Lithium + iodine → **lithium iodide**, LiI.
Iron + chlorine → **iron(III) chloride**, FeCl3.
Aluminium + chlorine → **aluminium chloride**, AlCl3.
Magnesium + chlorine → **magnesium chloride**, MgCl2.

callouts.p: Halide ions are always **1-**. Use as many halide ions as the metal ion's charge: 1+ needs one, 2+ needs two, 3+ needs three.

core.h: Halogens with Group 1 metals: sodium and chlorine
core.p: Hot sodium reacts vigorously with chlorine gas. This is a classic demonstration done in a fume cupboard.
bullets: Observation: the sodium burns with a **bright yellow-orange flame**.
A **white solid** forms - **sodium chloride**.
Word equation: sodium + chlorine → sodium chloride.
Balanced: **2Na(s) + Cl2(g) → 2NaCl(s)**.
Same pattern with bromine: 2Na + Br2 → 2NaBr; and iodine: 2Na + I2 → 2NaI.
Group 1 halides are **white solids** that dissolve in water to give **colourless** solutions.

callouts.p: Each Cl2 molecule gives **two** chloride ions, so a 1+ metal needs **2** atoms per Cl2: 2M + X2 → 2MX.

core.h: Halogens with iron: comparing the three
core.p: Heating iron wool in each halogen shows the decrease in reactivity down the group clearly. The vigour of the reaction (how brightly the iron glows and how fast it reacts) **decreases** from chlorine to bromine to iodine.
bullets: **Chlorine**: hot iron wool **glows brightly**; an **orange-brown solid**, iron(III) chloride, forms. 2Fe + 3Cl2 → 2FeCl3.
**Bromine** vapour: iron wool **glows, but less brightly**; iron(III) bromide forms. 2Fe + 3Br2 → 2FeBr3.
**Iodine** vapour: iron wool needs **strong heating** and **only glows faintly** / reacts slowly; iron(II) iodide forms. Fe + I2 → FeI2.
The trend in vigour shows **reactivity decreases down Group 7**.
Done in a **fume cupboard** because the halogens are toxic.

head: Halogen
Observation with hot iron wool
Product
Reactivity
rows: Faint glow, slow, needs strong heat

callouts.p: Iodine is not reactive enough to oxidise iron to iron(III), so it gives **FeI2**. If unsure in an exam, the key mark is the **trend in vigour**, not this detail.

core.p: When a metal reacts with a halogen, the metal atoms **lose** electrons and the halogen atoms **gain** them. The oppositely charged ions attract to form a giant **ionic lattice**.
bullets: Sodium atom 2.8.1 **loses 1 electron** → Na+ [2.8]+.
Chlorine atom 2.8.7 **gains 1 electron** → Cl- [2.8.8]-.
Both ions now have **full outer shells** (noble gas configurations).
Strong **electrostatic attraction** between Na+ and Cl- = ionic bond.
Half equations (Higher): Na → Na+ + e- and Cl2 + 2e- → 2Cl-.
The halogen is **reduced** (gains electrons); the metal is **oxidised** (loses electrons).

callouts.p: **Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain** of electrons. Metal halide formation is a **redox** reaction.

core.h: Predicting reactions of other halogens with metals
core.p: The specification asks you to **use the pattern to predict** the reactions of other halogens. Because every halogen has 7 outer electrons, they all react the **same way** - only the vigour changes.
bullets: **Fluorine** is above chlorine, so it reacts **even more vigorously** - most metals burst into flame in fluorine.
Fluorine + sodium → sodium fluoride: 2Na + F2 → 2NaF.
**Astatine** is below iodine, so it would react **even more slowly** than iodine.
Astatine + sodium → sodium astatide: 2Na + At2 → 2NaAt.
The products are always ionic **metal halides** containing **X-** ions.
Justify: 'reactivity decreases down the group, so...'

callouts.p: For a prediction mark you need the **direction** of change (more/less vigorous) and, for a second mark, the **reason** (position in group / trend).

core.p: Halogens react with hydrogen gas to form **hydrogen halides**. These are **covalent** molecules: hydrogen and the halogen **share** a pair of electrons. As with metals, the reaction becomes **less vigorous down the group**.
bullets: General equation: **H2 + X2 → 2HX**.
H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g) - hydrogen chloride.
H2(g) + Br2(g) → 2HBr(g) - hydrogen bromide.
H2(g) + I2(g) → 2HI(g) - hydrogen iodide.
**Fluorine** reacts explosively with hydrogen even in the cold and dark.
**Chlorine** reacts explosively in **sunlight** or with a flame; **bromine** needs **heating**; **iodine** reacts only slowly and incompletely even when **heated**.

head: Halogen

Product
rows: Slow and incomplete even when heated

callouts.p: One H2 and one X2 give **two** HX molecules. Always write **2HCl**, not HCl2.

core.p: Hydrogen chloride, hydrogen bromide and hydrogen iodide are all **colourless gases** at room temperature, made of small covalent molecules.
bullets: They are **very soluble in water**.
They give off **steamy (misty) fumes** in moist air as they dissolve in water vapour.
As pure dry gases they are **not acidic** - they are covalent molecules with no free H+ ions.
They are **toxic** and **corrosive**.
They have the same molecular pattern: H-X with one shared pair.

core.h: Hydrogen halides dissolve to form acids
core.p: Spec point 6.10: hydrogen halides **dissolve in water to form acidic solutions**. In water the molecules **split up (ionise)** to release **hydrogen ions, H+(aq)**, which make the solution acidic.
bullets: HCl(g) + water → H+(aq) + Cl-(aq): **hydrochloric acid**.
HBr(g) → H+(aq) + Br-(aq): **hydrobromic acid**.
HI(g) → H+(aq) + I-(aq): **hydroiodic acid**.
These solutions have a **low pH** (below 7; strongly acidic).
They turn **blue litmus red** and universal indicator **red**.
They react like typical acids, e.g. with metals, bases and carbonates.

callouts.p: A substance that releases **hydrogen ions, H+**, when dissolved in water, giving a solution with **pH less than 7**.

callouts.t: Hydrogen chloride is not hydrochloric acid
callouts.p: **Hydrogen chloride** is the gas HCl(g). **Hydrochloric acid** is its solution in water, HCl(aq). Use state symbols to show the difference.

core.h: Grade 9 extension: why water is needed
core.p: The acidity only appears when water is present, because water allows the molecule to **ionise**. This is a favourite high-demand question.
bullets: Hydrogen chloride dissolved in a non-aqueous solvent such as **methylbenzene** does **not** ionise.
So that solution has **no H+ ions** and does **not** behave as an acid (it does not turn dry litmus red or react with magnesium).
In water, HCl splits into H+(aq) and Cl-(aq) ions, so the solution **is acidic** and **conducts electricity**.
This shows it is the **H+ ion**, not the HCl molecule, that causes acidic properties.
The same applies to HBr and HI.

core.p: Using the pattern, you can predict the product and properties for fluorine and astatine.
bullets: Fluorine: H2 + F2 → 2HF, **hydrogen fluoride**; dissolves to form **hydrofluoric acid** (acidic).
Astatine: H2 + At2 → 2HAt, **hydrogen astatide**; would react **very slowly**, but its solution would be **acidic**.
Every hydrogen halide dissolves in water to release **H+(aq)** ions.
The vigour of formation decreases down the group because reactivity of the halogen decreases.
Name endings: hydrogen + ide (gas); hydro...ic acid (solution).

core.p: Pull the ideas together with these points; each tends to carry a mark.
bullets: Name the product correctly with the **-ide** ending.
Balance equations with **diatomic** halogens (X2).
Describe **observations** (flame colour, glowing, colour of solid) not just products.
State the **trend**: less vigorous down the group.
For acids: **dissolves in water**, releases **H+ ions**, **pH below 7**.
Mention the **fume cupboard** for any safety question.

analogy.p: Picture each halogen atom as a collector who needs just one more card (electron) to finish a set of eight. A metal like sodium is a person desperate to give one card away, so the swap happens eagerly and both walk away as charged ions stuck together by attraction - a metal halide. Hydrogen is less generous: it only agrees to share a card, so the two hold it jointly - a covalent hydrogen halide. Fluorine and chlorine are the hungriest collectors; iodine is lazier, so its swaps are slower. When the hydrogen halide is dropped into water, the water pulls the shared card away from hydrogen, leaving H+ free in the solution - that is what makes it acidic. Where it breaks down: electrons are not traded by choice, and the 'hunger' really depends on how strongly the nucleus attracts an incoming electron.

terms.d: An element in Group 7 of the periodic table, with 7 outer-shell electrons.
The 1- ion formed when a halogen atom gains one electron, e.g. Cl-, Br-, I-.
An ionic compound formed when a metal reacts with a halogen, e.g. sodium chloride NaCl.
An ionic compound formed from a metal (or ammonium) ion and a non-metal ion; metal halides are salts.
A covalent compound of hydrogen and a halogen, HX, e.g. hydrogen chloride HCl; a colourless gas.
The acidic solution formed when hydrogen chloride gas dissolves in water, HCl(aq).
To split up into ions; hydrogen halides ionise in water to form H+ and X- ions.
H+(aq); the ion responsible for acidic properties in aqueous solution.
A solution with a pH less than 7 that contains H+(aq) ions.
The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
Loss of electrons; the metal is oxidised when it forms a metal halide.
Gain of electrons; the halogen is reduced when it forms halide ions.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen at the same time.
Consisting of two atoms per molecule, as in Cl2, Br2 and I2.
How fast and energetically a reaction happens; it decreases down Group 7.

mistakes.w: Sodium + chlorine → sodium chlorine.
mistakes.r: The product is **sodium chloride** (-ide ending).

mistakes.w: Na + Cl → NaCl
mistakes.r: Chlorine is diatomic: **2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl**.

mistakes.w: H2 + Cl2 → H2Cl2 or HCl2
Hydrogen chloride gas is an acid.
mistakes.r: It forms an **acidic solution when it dissolves in water**, because it releases H+ ions.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen halides dissolve to form alkaline solutions.
mistakes.r: They form **acidic** solutions, pH less than 7.

mistakes.w: Iodine reacts more vigorously with iron than chlorine because it is bigger.
mistakes.r: Reactivity **decreases** down Group 7, so iodine reacts **less** vigorously than chlorine.

mistakes.w: Chlorine atoms lose electrons to form Cl+ ions.
mistakes.r: Chlorine atoms **gain** one electron to form **Cl-** ions.

mistakes.w: Sodium chloride forms as a yellow solid.
mistakes.r: The **flame** is yellow; sodium chloride is a **white** solid.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen chloride is ionic.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen chloride is a **covalent** molecule; it only forms ions when dissolved in water.

exam.q: Name the compound formed when potassium reacts with bromine.
model: Potassium bromide
exam.tip: Halogen changes -ine to -ide.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of sodium with chlorine.
model: Correct formulae: Na, Cl2, NaCl
Balanced: 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl
exam.tip: Cl2 is diatomic.

exam.q: Describe what you would see when hot sodium is placed in a jar of chlorine.
model: Burns with a (bright) yellow / orange flame
White solid forms
exam.tip: Observations, not names of products.

exam.q: Hot iron wool is placed in chlorine, then in bromine vapour, then in iodine vapour. Describe and explain the differences seen.
model: With chlorine iron glows brightly / reacts vigorously
With bromine less brightly / less vigorous
With iodine only faint glow / slow / needs more heating
Reactivity of halogens decreases down Group 7
exam.tip: Compare all three and state the trend.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of hydrogen with bromine and name the product.
model: H2 + Br2 → 2HBr
Hydrogen bromide
exam.tip: Two HBr molecules per H2.

exam.q: Hydrogen chloride gas is bubbled into water. State and explain the effect on the pH of the water.
model: pH decreases / falls below 7 / becomes acidic
Hydrogen chloride dissolves / ionises
Releases H+ ions (hydrochloric acid formed)
exam.tip: Link pH to H+ ions.

exam.q: Predict the name and formula of the compound formed when hydrogen reacts with fluorine, and state how the reaction would compare with chlorine.
model: Hydrogen fluoride
HF
More vigorous / explosive (even in dark) as fluorine is more reactive
exam.tip: Fluorine is at the top of the group: most reactive.

exam.q: Predict how astatine would react with hydrogen and what would happen if the product were dissolved in water.
model: Reacts very slowly / less vigorously than iodine
Forms hydrogen astatide, HAt
Dissolves to form an acidic solution / releases H+ ions
exam.tip: Same pattern as other halogens, but slowest.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of electrons, what happens when magnesium reacts with chlorine to form magnesium chloride. (Higher)
model: Magnesium atom loses 2 electrons to form Mg2+
Each chlorine atom gains 1 electron to form Cl-
Two chloride ions per magnesium ion: MgCl2
Ions attracted by electrostatic forces / ionic bonding; Mg oxidised, Cl reduced
exam.tip: Mention both ions and their charges.

exam.q: Describe the reactions of halogens with metals and with hydrogen, and explain how the products of the hydrogen reactions form acidic solutions. Refer to chlorine, bromine and iodine.
model: Halogens react with metals to form metal halides, e.g. 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl
With iron: chlorine most vigorous, then bromine, iodine slowest
Halogens react with hydrogen to form hydrogen halides, H2 + X2 → 2HX
Reactions with hydrogen less vigorous down the group (chlorine explosive in sunlight, iodine slow even when heated)
Hydrogen halides are colourless gases that dissolve in water
They ionise to release H+ ions, forming acidic solutions (pH below 7), e.g. hydrochloric acid
exam.tip: Cover both reaction types and the acid explanation for the top level.

exam.q: A student says that a solution of hydrogen chloride in methylbenzene would turn blue litmus red. Explain why the student is wrong.
model: Hydrogen chloride does not ionise in methylbenzene
So no H+ ions are present (it is only acidic in water)
exam.tip: Acidity needs H+ ions, which need water.

worked.q: Aluminium reacts with chlorine to form aluminium chloride. Write the formula and a balanced equation.
steps: Aluminium forms Al3+; chloride is Cl-.
To balance charges you need three Cl- for each Al3+, so the formula is AlCl3.
Unbalanced: Al + Cl2 → AlCl3.
Chlorine atoms: 2 on left, 3 on right. Lowest common multiple is 6, so use 3Cl2 and 2AlCl3.
Aluminium: 2 on right, so 2Al on left.
Check: Al 2 = 2; Cl 6 = 6.

worked.q: Predict the reaction of hydrogen with iodine, then explain why the product turns blue litmus red only when water is present.
steps: Iodine is low in Group 7, so it is less reactive than chlorine or bromine.
Prediction: reacts slowly and incompletely, even when heated.
Equation: H2 + I2 → 2HI, forming hydrogen iodide gas.
Dry HI is a covalent molecule with no free H+ ions, so it is not acidic.
In water, HI ionises: HI → H+(aq) + I-(aq).
The H+ ions make the solution acidic, so blue litmus turns red.
worked.ans: H2 + I2 → 2HI (slow); hydrogen iodide only gives acidic H+ ions when it dissolves and ionises in water.

worked.q: Use the data to predict an observation for fluorine with iron wool: chlorine - glows brightly; bromine - glows less brightly; iodine - faint glow.
steps: The vigour decreases from chlorine to iodine, so it increases going up the group.
Fluorine is above chlorine, so it is more reactive than chlorine.
So iron should react even more vigorously - it would burn or glow very brightly without much heating.
Product: iron fluoride (an ionic metal halide).
worked.ans: Iron would react more vigorously than with chlorine (burns very brightly), forming iron fluoride.

chem_edx.6.4.summary: A more reactive halogen will **displace** a less reactive halogen from a solution of its halide ions, so chlorine displaces bromide and iodide, and bromine displaces iodide, but iodine displaces neither. These reactions are **redox** reactions: the halogen molecule gains electrons and is reduced, while the halide ion loses electrons and is oxidised. Reactivity decreases down Group 7 because the atoms get bigger, the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is harder for the atom to attract and gain the one extra electron it needs.

core.h: What a halogen displacement reaction is
core.p: In a displacement reaction a **more reactive halogen takes the place of a less reactive halogen** in a compound. In GCSE practicals the halogen is added as an aqueous solution (chlorine water, bromine water or iodine solution) to a colourless solution of a metal halide, usually potassium chloride, potassium bromide or potassium iodide. If the added halogen is more reactive, it removes electrons from the halide ions and the less reactive halogen is released as its element, which shows up as a colour change.
bullets: **More reactive halogen + salt of less reactive halogen → salt of more reactive halogen + less reactive halogen**
The halide solutions (KCl, KBr, KI) are all **colourless** at the start
A reaction is shown by a **colour change** as the less reactive halogen is produced
If the added halogen is less reactive than the one in the salt, **no reaction** happens and the mixture just shows the colour of the halogen solution that was added
The metal (for example potassium) does not change: its ions are **spectator ions**
Displacement reactions are used to work out the **order of reactivity** of the halogens

callouts.p: A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound.
A halogen can only displace a halogen that is BELOW it in Group 7.

core.p: The experiment is usually done on a spotting tile or in test tubes. A few drops of each halogen solution are added to each halide solution, and any colour change is recorded. Because chlorine and bromine are toxic, this is done in a **well ventilated room or fume cupboard**, wearing **eye protection**.
bullets: Place a few drops of potassium chloride, potassium bromide and potassium iodide solutions in separate wells of a **spotting tile**
Add a few drops of **chlorine water** to each, then repeat with **bromine water** and **iodine solution**
Record whether a colour change happens for each combination
A halogen is not added to its own halide (for example chlorine water to potassium chloride), because nothing could be learned
Compare with a **control**: the colour of the halogen solution added to water, so a real colour change can be identified
Optional: shake with an organic solvent such as cyclohexane; iodine dissolves to give a **purple** layer and bromine an **orange** layer, which makes the result clearer

callouts.p: Chlorine and bromine are toxic and corrosive. Use small volumes, a fume cupboard or good ventilation, and eye protection.

core.p: Marks often depend on stating the correct colour of the solution formed. The colour in a displacement reaction comes from the **halogen produced**, not the halide ions, because halide ions are colourless in solution.
bullets: Chlorine water: **very pale green** (often looks almost colourless)
Bromine water / bromine in solution: **orange** (yellow-orange when dilute)
Iodine solution: **brown** (yellow-brown when dilute)
Chloride, bromide and iodide ions in solution: **colourless**
So a solution turning **orange** means bromine has formed; turning **brown** means iodine has formed

head: Substance in solution
Colour
rows: Cl-, Br-, I- ions (e.g. KCl, KBr, KI)

callouts.t: Say what colour it turns to
callouts.p: Write 'the colourless solution turns orange', not just 'it changes colour'. Examiners want the final colour.

core.p: Putting all the results together gives the grid below. Every reaction happens where the halogen added is **higher up** Group 7 than the halide in the solution.
bullets: Chlorine displaces bromide (orange) and iodide (brown)
Bromine displaces iodide (brown) but not chloride
Iodine displaces neither chloride nor bromide
Order of reactivity found: **chlorine > bromine > iodine**

core.p: You should be able to write word equations and balanced symbol equations for each displacement reaction. Remember halogens exist as **diatomic molecules** (Cl2, Br2, I2), so two halide ions are needed for each halogen molecule, which is why potassium halides appear with a 2 in front.
bullets: chlorine + potassium bromide → potassium chloride + bromine
Cl2(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br2(aq)
chlorine + potassium iodide → potassium chloride + iodine
Cl2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + I2(aq)
bromine + potassium iodide → potassium bromide + iodine
Br2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KBr(aq) + I2(aq)
The same pattern works with sodium halides, for example Cl2 + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br2
With a Group 2 halide such as magnesium bromide, the formula already has two halide ions: Cl2 + MgBr2 → MgCl2 + Br2

callouts.p: Never write Cl or Br as a product or reactant on its own: the elements are Cl2, Br2 and I2.

core.p: Because the potassium (or sodium) ions do not change, they are **spectator ions** and can be left out. The **ionic equation** shows only the species that actually react: the halogen molecule and the halide ions.
bullets: Cl2(aq) + 2Br-(aq) → 2Cl-(aq) + Br2(aq)
Cl2(aq) + 2I-(aq) → 2Cl-(aq) + I2(aq)
Br2(aq) + 2I-(aq) → 2Br-(aq) + I2(aq)
Check that **charges balance**: two negative charges on the left and two on the right
Check **atoms balance**: two chlorine atoms on each side, two bromine atoms on each side

callouts.p: Write the full equation, split soluble ionic compounds into ions, cross out the ions that appear unchanged on both sides, and write what is left.

core.p: Redox means **reduction and oxidation happening at the same time**. In a halogen displacement reaction, electrons are transferred from the halide ions to the halogen molecules. Using OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons), the halide ion is oxidised and the halogen molecule is reduced.
bullets: The **halogen molecule gains electrons** and becomes halide ions, so it is **reduced**
The **halide ion loses electrons** and becomes halogen molecules, so it is **oxidised**
Because both happen together, the reaction is a **redox reaction**
Example: in Cl2 + 2Br- → 2Cl- + Br2, chlorine is reduced and bromide ions are oxidised
The species that is reduced (Cl2) is the **oxidising agent**; the species that is oxidised (Br-) is the **reducing agent**
Potassium ions are neither oxidised nor reduced: they are spectators

callouts.p: Oxidation is the loss of electrons. Reduction is the gain of electrons.
A reaction in which both oxidation and reduction take place.
