core.p: A redox reaction can be split into two **half equations**, one showing the reduction and one showing the oxidation. Electrons are written as e-. The number of electrons lost in the oxidation half equation must equal the number gained in the reduction half equation.
bullets: Reduction of chlorine: Cl2 + 2e- → 2Cl-
Reduction of bromine: Br2 + 2e- → 2Br-
Oxidation of bromide: 2Br- → Br2 + 2e-
Oxidation of iodide: 2I- → I2 + 2e-
Electrons appear on the **left** in a reduction (gained) and on the **right** in an oxidation (lost)
Adding the two half equations and cancelling the electrons gives the ionic equation: Cl2 + 2e- + 2I- → 2Cl- + I2 + 2e- becomes Cl2 + 2I- → 2Cl- + I2

callouts.p: In 2Br- → Br2 + 2e-, the left has a total charge of 2- and the right has 0 + 2- = 2-. Always check the total charge is the same on both sides.

core.p: The displacement results show that **reactivity decreases going down Group 7**. Fluorine is the most reactive halogen and astatine would be the least reactive. This is the opposite trend to Group 1, where reactivity increases down the group.
bullets: Order: **fluorine > chlorine > bromine > iodine > astatine**
Fluorine is too reactive and dangerous to use in school displacement experiments
A halogen higher in the group can displace any halide below it
Predictions: fluorine would displace chloride, bromide and iodide; astatine would not displace any of the other halides
Iodine could displace astatide ions, because iodine is above astatine

callouts.p: Group 1: reactivity increases down the group (outer electron lost more easily). Group 7: reactivity decreases down the group (extra electron gained less easily).

core.h: Explaining the trend using electronic configuration
core.p: All halogen atoms have **7 electrons in their outer shell**. When a halogen reacts it **gains one electron** to get a full outer shell and form a halide ion with a 1- charge. The more easily the atom attracts that extra electron, the more reactive the halogen is. Going down the group this becomes harder.
bullets: Electronic configurations: F 2.7, Cl 2.8.7 (Br and I also have 7 outer electrons)
Going down the group the atoms have **more occupied shells**, so the atomic radius increases
The outer shell is **further from the nucleus**
There is **more shielding** by inner shells of electrons between the nucleus and the outer shell
So the **attraction between the nucleus and an incoming electron is weaker**
An electron is **gained less easily**, so the halogen is **less reactive**
Although the nuclear charge increases down the group, the effect of extra distance and shielding outweighs it

callouts.p: More shells → outer shell further from nucleus and more shielded → weaker attraction for an extra electron → electron gained less easily → less reactive.
You only need to show full configurations for the first 20 elements. For bromine and iodine it is enough to say they have 7 outer electrons and more shells.

core.p: Displacement happens because the more reactive halogen has a **stronger attraction for electrons** than the less reactive one. Chlorine atoms attract electrons more strongly than bromine atoms, so chlorine molecules pull an electron away from each bromide ion. The bromide ions lose their extra electron and pair up as Br2 molecules.
bullets: The more reactive halogen is the **better oxidising agent** (it gains electrons more readily)
Halide ions of the less reactive halogen hold their extra electron **less tightly**, so they lose it
Iodide ions lose electrons most easily, so iodide is oxidised by both chlorine and bromine
Chloride ions hold their electron tightly, so neither bromine nor iodine can oxidise them
This is why the order of displacement exactly matches the order of reactivity

callouts.p: Link the observation (colour change) to the product formed, to the reactivity order, and then to electron gain in terms of atom size, shielding and attraction.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to predict a reaction you have not seen, such as one involving fluorine or astatine, or a different metal halide. Use the position in the group to decide, then write the equation using the same pattern.
bullets: Fluorine + sodium chloride: reaction, because fluorine is above chlorine (F2 + 2NaCl → 2NaF + Cl2, in theory; in reality fluorine reacts with water too)
Astatine + potassium iodide: **no reaction**, because astatine is below iodine
Chlorine + sodium astatide: reaction, astatine formed: Cl2 + 2NaAt → 2NaCl + At2
Bromine + potassium chloride: **no reaction**, the solution simply stays orange from the bromine water added
Always state **which halogen is more reactive** as the reason

callouts.t: No reaction still has a colour
callouts.p: When bromine water is added to potassium chloride, the mixture looks orange, but that is just the bromine added. There is no colour change, so no reaction.

analogy.p: Think of each halogen as a team in a tug-of-war over one electron. A smaller atom is like a strong team standing close to the rope: its pull (the nucleus) is near the electron with nothing in the way. A bigger atom is like a team standing far back behind a crowd (the inner shells), so its pull is weaker. When chlorine meets bromide ions, chlorine's team wins and takes the electrons, so bromine is left as Br2. Bromine's team can never beat chlorine's, so it cannot take the electrons back from chloride. Where it breaks down: real atoms do not choose to compete, the 'pull' is electrostatic attraction between the positive nucleus and negative electron, and the nuclear charge actually gets bigger down the group even though the overall attraction for the outer electron gets weaker.

terms.d: An element in Group 7 of the periodic table, existing as diatomic molecules such as Cl2, Br2 and I2.
A negative ion with a 1- charge formed when a halogen atom gains one electron, for example Cl-, Br-, I-.
A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound.
A molecule made of two atoms joined by a covalent bond, for example Cl2.
The loss of electrons.
The gain of electrons.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen at the same time.
A substance that causes oxidation by accepting electrons; it is itself reduced.
A substance that causes reduction by donating electrons; it is itself oxidised.
An equation showing either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction, with electrons written as e-.
An equation showing only the ions and molecules that take part in a reaction, with spectator ions left out.
An ion present in the reaction mixture that does not change during the reaction.
The reduction in attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons caused by inner shells of electrons.
A measure of the size of an atom; it increases down a group as more shells are added.
The arrangement of electrons in shells around the nucleus, for example chlorine is 2.8.7.
How readily an element takes part in a chemical reaction; for halogens, how easily the atom gains an electron.

mistakes.r: Bromine is produced, so the solution turns orange. Brown shows iodine has been produced.

mistakes.r: Halogens get less reactive down the group because the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so an electron is gained less easily.

mistakes.r: Potassium ions are spectator ions; they are neither oxidised nor reduced.

mistakes.r: Br2 + 2e- → 2Br-; the electron and the ions must have their charges.

exam.q: Explain why there is no reaction when iodine solution is added to potassium bromide solution.
model: Iodine is less reactive than bromine
So iodine cannot displace bromine (from bromide ions)
exam.tip: Use comparative language: 'less reactive than'.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation for the reaction between bromine and potassium iodide.
model: Correct formulae: Br2, KI, KBr, I2
Balanced: Br2 + 2KI → 2KBr + I2
exam.tip: Remember the 2 in front of KI and KBr.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the reaction between chlorine and bromide ions.
model: Cl2 + 2Br- → 2Cl- + Br2
Correct charges and balancing
exam.tip: Leave out the potassium ions; they are spectators.

exam.q: (Higher) Chlorine reacts with potassium iodide solution. Explain, in terms of electrons, why this is a redox reaction.
model: Chlorine (molecules) gain electrons
So chlorine is reduced
Iodide ions lose electrons
So iodide ions are oxidised; both happen at once so it is redox
exam.tip: Name the species precisely: chlorine molecules and iodide ions, not 'iodine'.

exam.q: (Higher) Write the half equation for the oxidation of iodide ions.
exam.tip: Electrons go on the right-hand side for oxidation.

exam.q: (Higher) Identify the oxidising agent in the reaction Br2 + 2I- → 2Br- + I2. Give a reason.
model: Bromine / Br2
It gains electrons / is reduced / accepts electrons from iodide ions
exam.tip: The oxidising agent is the one that is reduced.

exam.q: Explain why chlorine is more reactive than bromine. Refer to electronic configurations in your answer.
model: Both have 7 electrons in the outer shell / need to gain one electron
Chlorine atom is smaller / has fewer shells (2.8.7)
Outer shell closer to the nucleus and less shielding
So stronger attraction for an extra electron, so electron gained more easily
exam.tip: Always end with 'gains an electron more easily'.

exam.q: Astatine is below iodine in Group 7. Predict whether astatine would react with sodium iodide solution. Explain your answer.
model: No reaction
Astatine is less reactive than iodine (as reactivity decreases down the group)
exam.tip: Prediction marks need a reason linked to position in the group.

exam.q: A student is given solutions of chlorine, bromine and iodine, and solutions of potassium chloride, potassium bromide and potassium iodide. Describe how the student could use these to find the order of reactivity of the halogens, and explain the results expected.
model: Add a few drops of each halogen solution to each halide solution (e.g. on a spotting tile)
Look for a colour change / compare with halogen in water as a control
Chlorine with bromide turns orange; chlorine with iodide turns brown
Bromine with iodide turns brown; bromine with chloride no change
Iodine with chloride or bromide no change
So order of reactivity is chlorine > bromine > iodine, as a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one
exam.tip: Level-marked: include method, observations with colours, and a conclusion with the reason.

exam.q: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen. Explain why, in terms of atomic structure.
model: Fluorine has the smallest atoms / fewest shells (2.7)
Outer shell closest to nucleus with least shielding
Strongest attraction for an extra electron so gains an electron most easily
exam.tip: Same chain of reasoning as for chlorine and bromine.

worked.q: Chlorine gas is bubbled into sodium bromide solution. Describe what is seen and write the word, symbol and ionic equations.
steps: Chlorine is above bromine in Group 7, so it is more reactive and will displace bromine.
Bromine is formed, so the colourless solution turns orange.
Word equation: chlorine + sodium bromide → sodium chloride + bromine
Symbol equation: Cl2 + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br2 (two Br needed to make one Br2)
Sodium ions do not change, so they are spectator ions and are removed.
Ionic equation: Cl2 + 2Br- → 2Cl- + Br2
worked.ans: The solution turns orange; Cl2 + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br2; ionic: Cl2 + 2Br- → 2Cl- + Br2.

worked.q: (Higher) For Br2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → 2KBr(aq) + I2(aq), write the half equations and identify what is oxidised and what is reduced.
steps: Remove spectator K+ ions: Br2 + 2I- → 2Br- + I2
Bromine molecule becomes bromide ions, gaining electrons: Br2 + 2e- → 2Br-
Gaining electrons is reduction, so bromine is reduced.
Iodide ions become an iodine molecule, losing electrons: 2I- → I2 + 2e-
Losing electrons is oxidation, so iodide ions are oxidised.
Check: 2 electrons lost equals 2 electrons gained; adding the half equations gives the ionic equation.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why bromine is less reactive than chlorine but more reactive than iodine.
steps: All three atoms have 7 electrons in their outer shell and react by gaining one electron.
Going down the group, from chlorine to bromine to iodine, the atoms have more electron shells.
So the outer shell is further from the nucleus and there is more shielding by inner electrons.
The attraction between the nucleus and an incoming electron gets weaker down the group.
Bromine atoms attract an extra electron less strongly than chlorine but more strongly than iodine.
worked.ans: Bromine gains an electron less easily than chlorine (bigger atom, more shielding) but more easily than iodine (smaller atom, less shielding), so its reactivity is in between.

chem_edx.6.5.summary: The noble gases in Group 0 (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon) are **chemically inert** because their atoms have a **full outer shell of electrons**, so they have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons. Their uses depend on this inertness together with **low density** and **non-flammability**, for example helium in balloons, argon in filament lamps and welding, and neon in signs. Going down the group the atoms get larger, so **boiling point and density increase**, and this pattern can be used to predict the properties of other noble gases.

core.p: The noble gases make up **Group 0**, the column on the far right of the periodic table. They are all non-metals and are all **colourless gases at room temperature**. They exist as single atoms, so they are described as **monatomic**, unlike other gaseous elements such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine, which form diatomic molecules.
bullets: Members in order down the group: **helium (He), neon (Ne), argon (Ar), krypton (Kr), xenon (Xe), radon (Rn)**
All are **colourless, odourless gases** at room temperature
They are **monatomic**: the formula of helium is He, not He2
Argon makes up about 1% of the air; helium is found in natural gas deposits
Radon is **radioactive**
The group is called Group 0 (not Group 8) because the atoms have no tendency to lose or gain electrons

callouts.p: Noble gases exist as single, separate atoms because they do not bond with each other.

core.p: The key feature of every noble gas atom is that its **outer shell is full**. Helium has only one shell, which is full with 2 electrons. All the other noble gases have **8 electrons in their outer shell**, often called a stable octet.
bullets: Helium: **2** (outer shell full with 2 electrons)
Krypton, xenon and radon also have 8 electrons in their outer shell
Other elements react to **achieve** this same electronic arrangement, for example Na+ (2.8) has the same arrangement as neon, and Cl- (2.8.8) has the same arrangement as argon

callouts.p: Do not say every noble gas has 8 outer electrons. Helium has 2, but its outer (first) shell is still full.

core.h: Why the noble gases are inert
core.p: Atoms react by **losing, gaining or sharing electrons** to get a full outer shell. Noble gas atoms **already have a full outer shell**, which is a very **stable** arrangement. They have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons, so they are **chemically inert** (extremely unreactive) and do not easily form molecules or compounds.
bullets: Full outer shell = **stable electronic arrangement**
No need to **lose** electrons (unlike Group 1 metals)
No need to **gain** electrons (unlike Group 7 halogens)
No need to **share** electrons to form covalent bonds
So they do not form ions or molecules, and exist as **separate atoms**
This explains both their **inertness** and why they are **monatomic**

callouts.p: Chemically unreactive: does not readily take part in chemical reactions.
Noble gases are inert because they have a full outer shell of electrons, so they do not easily lose, gain or share electrons.

core.h: Inert does not mean never reacts
core.p: At GCSE level the noble gases are described as inert, and you should treat them as unreactive. Chemists have made a small number of compounds of the heavier noble gases, mainly xenon, under special conditions, but helium, neon and argon are not known to form stable compounds in normal conditions.
bullets: Use the words **inert** or **very unreactive** in answers
Do not write that the noble gases 'have no electrons to react with'; they have electrons, but a full outer shell
Their lack of reactivity is a **chemical property**; their boiling points and densities are **physical properties**

callouts.p: 'Noble gases are stable because they have 8 electrons' loses marks: say 'a full outer shell' (helium has 2).

core.p: The uses of the noble gases come from three key properties. In exam answers you must **link the use to the property** that makes it suitable, not just list uses.
bullets: **Inertness**: they do not react with other substances, even at high temperatures
**Low density**: helium in particular is much less dense than air, so it floats
**Non-flammability**: they do not burn, so they are safe to use near flames, sparks or heat
Some noble gases **glow with distinctive colours** when an electric current is passed through them at low pressure

core.p: Helium is the second least dense gas (only hydrogen is less dense). A balloon filled with helium is **less dense than the surrounding air**, so it rises. Hydrogen is even less dense, but it is **highly flammable** and forms explosive mixtures with air. Helium is **non-flammable and inert**, so it is much safer.
bullets: Helium density about **0.18 g/dm3**, air about **1.2 g/dm3** at room temperature
Low density → balloon or airship **floats/rises**
Non-flammable → **no risk of fire or explosion**, unlike hydrogen
Inert → does not react with the balloon material or the air
Helium is also used in weather balloons for the same reasons

callouts.p: For 'Explain why helium is used in airships', give BOTH low density (less dense than air) AND non-flammable / safer than hydrogen.

core.h: Argon in filament lamps and welding
core.p: In a filament lamp the thin tungsten filament gets **white hot**. If it were surrounded by air, the oxygen would react with the hot metal and the filament would quickly burn through. Filling the bulb with **argon**, which is inert, means the filament does not react, so the bulb lasts much longer. In welding, a stream of argon is blown over the hot metal to keep oxygen in the air away from it.
bullets: Filament lamps: argon is **inert**, so the very hot filament **does not react / burn**
Without argon, oxygen would **oxidise** the filament and it would break
Welding: argon acts as a **shield gas**, preventing the hot metal reacting with oxygen
Argon is cheap compared with other noble gases because it is about 1% of air
Argon is denser than air, which helps it form a protective blanket over the weld

callouts.p: The reason is that argon is inert so the hot filament cannot react with it, while air would contain oxygen that reacts with the filament.

core.p: When an electric current is passed through neon at low pressure in a glass tube, the gas **glows a bright red-orange colour**. Because neon is inert it does not react inside the tube, so the sign lasts a long time. Other noble gases glow with different colours and are also used in lighting.
bullets: Neon glows **red-orange** when electricity passes through it
It is **inert**, so it does not react with the electrodes or glass
Used for **advertising signs** and some indicator lights
Other coloured 'neon' signs often contain other noble gases or coatings

core.p: The physical properties of the noble gases change in a regular way going down the group. You need to know the pattern for **boiling point** and **density**, and be able to use the pattern to **predict** values for other noble gases. Both increase down the group.
bullets: **Boiling point increases** going down the group
**Melting point increases** going down the group too
**Density increases** going down the group
**Atomic radius increases** going down the group (more shells)
**Relative atomic mass increases** going down the group
All boiling points are **very low**, which is why they are all gases at room temperature

callouts.p: Going down Group 0, boiling point and density both increase.

core.p: Going down the group, each atom has **more electron shells** and a larger mass, so the atoms are **bigger and heavier**. The weak **forces of attraction between the atoms** get stronger as the atoms get bigger, so **more energy** is needed to overcome them, giving a higher boiling point. Density increases mainly because each atom has a **greater mass**, while the same volume of any gas (at the same temperature and pressure) contains about the same number of atoms.
bullets: More shells → **larger atoms** → **stronger forces of attraction between atoms**
Stronger forces → more energy needed to separate the atoms → **higher boiling point**
The forces between noble gas atoms are **very weak**, so all boiling points are well below 0 °C
Boiling a noble gas does **not break any bonds within atoms**; it only overcomes attractions between separate atoms
Heavier atoms → more mass in the same volume → **higher density**
Helium (0.18 g/dm3) and neon (0.90 g/dm3) are less dense than air; argon and the heavier noble gases are denser than air

callouts.p: Noble gases are monatomic, so boiling involves overcoming forces between atoms, not breaking covalent bonds.

core.h: Using the pattern to predict properties
core.p: Exam questions often give a table with one value missing and ask you to **predict** it. The answer must fit the trend: it should lie **between** the values of the elements above and below. Examiners usually accept any value in a sensible range rather than one exact number.
bullets: Find the elements above and below the missing one
The missing value must be **between** these two values
Look at the size of the gaps: the differences are not always equal, so pick a value that fits the pattern
Example: if argon boils at -186 °C and xenon at -108 °C, krypton should boil between these, for example about -150 °C (actual -153 °C)
For the last element (radon), predict a value **higher** than xenon, following the trend
State the physical state: a noble gas with a boiling point below 20 °C is a **gas at room temperature**

callouts.p: Write 'boiling point increases down the group, so krypton's must be between -186 °C and -108 °C'. A number with a reason is safer than a number alone.

core.p: It helps to see Group 0 alongside the other groups in this topic. The reactive groups react in order to reach the electronic arrangement that the noble gases already have.
bullets: Group 1 atoms **lose** 1 electron to get a noble gas configuration; reactivity increases down the group
Group 7 atoms **gain** 1 electron to get a noble gas configuration; reactivity decreases down the group
Group 0 atoms already have a full outer shell, so they **do not react**
Boiling point increases down both Group 7 and Group 0, but decreases down Group 1

analogy.p: Imagine atoms are collectors trying to complete a page in a sticker album (the outer shell). Group 1 atoms have one spare sticker they are desperate to give away, and Group 7 atoms are one sticker short and desperate to get one, so they trade (react) eagerly. Noble gas atoms already have a completed page, so they have no reason to swap with anyone: they are inert. The bigger albums further down the group are heavier and 'stickier' towards each other, which is like the heavier noble gases having higher densities and boiling points. Where it breaks down: atoms do not 'want' anything, the stability comes from the energy of the electron arrangement, and the forces between noble gas atoms are physical attractions, not trading.

mistakes.w: Noble gases are unreactive because they have 8 electrons.
mistakes.r: Noble gases are unreactive because they have a full outer shell (helium has 2 outer electrons), so they do not easily lose, gain or share electrons.

mistakes.w: Helium is used in balloons because it is light.
mistakes.r: Helium has a lower density than air (and is non-flammable).

mistakes.w: Argon is used in light bulbs because it does not conduct electricity / it glows.
mistakes.r: Argon is inert, so the hot filament does not react with it (it would react with oxygen in air and burn away).

mistakes.w: Boiling point decreases down Group 0.
mistakes.r: Boiling point increases down Group 0.

mistakes.w: Noble gases form diatomic molecules like He2.
mistakes.r: Noble gases are monatomic: they exist as single atoms (He, Ne, Ar).

mistakes.w: Boiling point increases because stronger covalent bonds have to be broken.
mistakes.r: There are no covalent bonds; the forces of attraction between atoms get stronger as atoms get larger, so more energy is needed.

mistakes.w: Helium is used in airships because it is less dense than hydrogen.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen is less dense than helium; helium is used because it is non-flammable and still much less dense than air.

worked.q: The table shows boiling points: helium -269 °C, neon -246 °C, argon -186 °C, krypton ?, xenon -108 °C. Predict the boiling point of krypton and explain your answer.
steps: Identify the trend: boiling point increases (becomes less negative) going down the group.
Krypton is between argon and xenon, so its boiling point must be between -186 °C and -108 °C.
The gaps get roughly similar in size lower down, so a value near the middle is sensible: about -150 °C.
Explanation: krypton atoms are larger than argon atoms but smaller than xenon atoms, so the forces between atoms are in between.
worked.ans: About -150 °C (any value between -186 °C and -108 °C); the actual value is -153 °C.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why airships were once filled with hydrogen but are now filled with helium.
steps: Both gases have a much lower density than air, so an airship filled with either gas will rise.
Hydrogen is the least dense gas, so it gives slightly more lift.
However, hydrogen is highly flammable and can form explosive mixtures with air.
Helium is a noble gas with a full outer shell, so it is inert and non-flammable.
Therefore helium is much safer, even though it is slightly denser than hydrogen.
worked.ans: Helium is used because it is less dense than air (so the airship floats) and, unlike hydrogen, it is inert and non-flammable, so there is no fire or explosion risk.

worked.q: Using the density values He 0.18, Ne 0.90, Ar 1.78 g/dm3 and air 1.2 g/dm3, explain which of these noble gases could be used to make a balloon float in air.
steps: A balloon floats if the gas inside is less dense than air.
Helium (0.18) is less dense than air (1.2), so it floats well.
Neon (0.90) is also less dense than air, so it would float, but with less lift than helium.
Argon (1.78) is denser than air, so an argon balloon would sink.
Helium is chosen in practice because it gives most lift and is inert and non-flammable.
worked.ans: Helium (and, in theory, neon) are less dense than air so would float; argon is denser than air so would sink.
